abstract.para: CPU shielding is the practice of reserving specific CPUs on a multi-core system strictly for high-priority or real-time tasks. It works by isolating these designated CPUs from general user processes, standard system services, and non-critical kernel threads.

topic.para: In a standard, unshielded Linux environment, the kernel's scheduler freely migrates processes across all available CPUs to balance the load. While this is efficient for general computing, it introduces unpredictability. If a standard background service or a kernel interrupt is scheduled on the same CPU as a critical real-time task, it forces the real-time task to wait. This waiting period introduces latency.

By implementing a CPU shield, you guarantee that only the specific workloads you authorize are allowed to execute on the shielded processors. This ensures deterministic execution times and eliminates latency spikes caused by resource contention, which is essential for real-time applications.

important.title: The legacy cset
important.para: The legacy cset command-line utility relies on the older cgroups v1 hierarchy and is no longer supported in &productnameshort; &productnumber;. All CPU isolation and thread assignment must be managed using &systemd; configuration files and commands.

section.title: How does CPU shielding work?
section.para: In &productnameshort; &productnumber;, &systemd; serves as the central manager for all system resources, including CPU allocation. It interacts directly with the kernel's cgroups v2 cpuset controller to assign specific CPUs to services and processes.

&systemd; natively supports the cpuset controller under the unified cgroups v2 hierarchy. Resource distribution in cgroups v2 follows a top-down model across the system hierarchy. &systemd; automatically creates top-level units, including init.scope, system.slice, user.slice, and machine.slice. To establish a shield, you configure AllowedCPUs on these default units to restrict them to non-shielded CPUs. You then create a custom workload slice assigned to the remaining shielded CPUs. &systemd; manages these resource boundaries directly without external utilities.
